Gish, MD Realizing functional cure at scale will take more than new drugs; it requires infrastructure, testing, and patient engagement working in concert. This episode closes the series with a roadmap for that shift. Advertisement Episodes in this series Previous slideNext slide EP. 1 Understanding the Immune Pathophysiology Driving Chronic Hepatitis B EP. 2 Hepatitis B Epidemiology: Closing the Screening and Diagnosis Gap EP. 3 Monitoring Disease Progression and Liver Cancer Risk in Hepatitis B EP. 4 Quantitative HBsAg Testing and the Path to Finite-Duration Therapy EP. 5 Unmet Needs and Long-Term Antiviral Safety in Hepatitis B Care EP. 6 Why Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C Cures Are Fundamentally Different EP. 7 The Next Frontier in Hepatitis B Functional and Virologic Cure EP. 8 Rethinking Standard of Care and the Promise of Functional Cure EP. 9 How Bepirovirsen Targets the Hepatitis B Viral Lifecycle EP. 10 Inside the Be-Well Trials: Design, Population, and Patient Selection EP. 11 Weighing Efficacy and Safety Data for an Emerging Hepatitis B Therapy EP. 12 Capsid Assembly Modulators and the Case for Combination Therapy EP. 13 Can Innate Immune Agonists Help Deliver Hepatitis B Cure? EP. 14 Therapeutic Vaccines and the Global Divide in E-Antigen Disease Now Playing EP. 15 Preparing Practices for the Next Era of Hepatitis B Care In "Preparing Practices for the Next Era of Hepatitis B Care," our experts close the series by outlining what practices, payers, and patients each need to do next. Dr. Chung asks what operational changes practices should prioritize to prepare for an expanding hepatitis B treatment landscape, and closes with a broader question about the most important remaining barriers to realizing functional cure at scale, spanning testing, payer policy, and patient engagement. Dr. Gish says embracing bepirovirsen as a major step forward matters, but so does building infrastructure to manage these patients, noting that some of his own clinics are booked four months out, which is not workable for launching a complex new therapy. He believes practices need to train physician colleagues, nurse practitioners, and physician assistants, prepare patients to use telemedicine, and lean on specialty pharmacies and infusion centers as partners in this expanding treatment model. Asked about the biggest remaining barriers, Dr. Gish offers five interconnected priorities. First is test-and-treat, extending the same urgency already applied to hepatitis C and HIV so patients are not allowed to get sicker before treatment begins, while also taking stigma, discrimination, and quality of life seriously through shared decision-making. Second is embedding quantitative surface antigen testing into every patient's workup, alongside emerging tests like quantitative HBV RNA and correlated antigen. Third is using the functional cure concept itself to bring patients into treatment and prepare them for that outcome. Fourth is community education about this hope and progress. Together, he says, these build toward a fifth pillar: growing patient interest in treatment once they understand finite therapy and functional cure are real possibilities. Dr. Gish closes by highlighting the Hepatitis B Foundation's advocacy work on payer policy, treatment access, and patient storytelling, calling it a central pillar supporting this broader five-part structure. Dr. Chung thanks Dr. Gish for his insights before concluding the program. Thank you for watching this AJMC Insights series on chronic hepatitis B. content: 173 new news items in the last 24 hours ECDC calls for systematic prenatal screening for HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis across Europe 2eu.brussels 29 September 2026, 10:49 EU Gustavo Fring / Pexels Always see our news on Google The new European standards aim to ensure that infections that can be transmitted from parent to child are detected early enough for intervention and treatment. ECDC reports that in 2024, 196 HIV diagnoses attributed to vertical transmission and 140 confirmed cases of congenital syphilis were reported in the EU and EEA, while data for hepatitis B remain incomplete in many countries. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control has published a common set of standards for prenatal screening for HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis, with the objective of reducing transmission of these infections from parent to child and making the quality of services comparable across EU and EEA countries. The document does not introduce new legal obligations for national healthcare systems, but establishes what ECDC considers quality care, what outcomes should be monitored and through which indicators the functioning of programmes can be assessed. In brief 1.The standards cover prenatal screening for HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis and aim for detection sufficiently early to prevent vertical transmission. 2.ECDC reports 196 HIV diagnoses attributed to vertical transmission in the EU and EEA in 2024, of which 147 were recorded among migrants. 3.In the same year, 140 confirmed cases of congenital syphilis were reported, almost twice as many as in 2023. 4.For hepatitis B, European data on the route of transmission are much more incomplete, limiting precise assessment of vertical transmission. 5.The standards are built around quality requirements, measurable indicators and targets that can be audited by health systems. The document starts from the fact that vertical transmission of the three infections can largely be prevented if diagnosis is made on time and the pregnant person quickly enters care. Prenatal screening thus becomes the first link in a chain that includes confirmation of the diagnosis, clinical assessment, treatment of the pregnant person, the interventions needed for the newborn and subsequent medical follow-up. ECDC addresses HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis together because all three can be transmitted in connection with pregnancy or childbirth, but prevention differs from one infection to another. For HIV, antiretroviral treatment and appropriate management of pregnancy can drastically reduce the risk of transmission. For hepatitis B, identifying the infection allows prophylactic interventions for the newborn and, in certain situations, antiviral treatment during pregnancy. In syphilis, early diagnosis and antibiotic treatment can prevent transmission to the fetus and severe complications. The data presented by ECDC show that the problem has not disappeared in Europe. In 2024, EU and EEA countries reported 196 new HIV diagnoses attributed to vertical transmission. Of these, 147, or 75%, were reported among migrants, defined by ECDC as people whose country of origin differs from the country reporting the diagnosis. This figure must be interpreted with caution. It does not mean that all 147 transmissions occurred within European healthcare systems. Data on diagnosis and country of origin do not automatically establish where the infection occurred. ECDC nevertheless uses the distribution to show why screening programmes must also be accessible to people who enter the healthcare system late, including migrants and other vulnerable groups. Congenital syphilis provides a different epidemiological signal. In 2024, 140 confirmed cases were reported in 28 EU and EEA countries, equivalent to a rate of 4.7 cases per 100,000 live births. The reported number almost doubled compared with the previous year, prompting ECDC once again to prioritise prevention of transmission during pregnancy. For the 63 cases of congenital syphilis for which information on the mother’s country of birth was available, it differed from the reporting country in 17 instances. The proportion is much lower than that observed in the HIV data, showing that there is no single epidemiological profile common to all three infections. In the case of hepatitis B, the main data problem is incompleteness. Information on the route of transmission was available for only 24% of acute cases reported in 2023 and 9% of chronic cases. Among acute cases with available information, approximately 1% were attributed to vertical transmission. The picture is different for chronic hepatitis B. Among the 1,421 newly diagnosed cases for which the route of transmission was known, vertical transmission accounted for 39% and was the most frequently identified route. In 91% of these cases, however, the infection was classified as imported, meaning that transmission had occurred in the country of origin, not in the European country that reported the diagnosis. This contrast explains why prenatal screening is treated both as a medical intervention and as an issue of access to services. A person may enter a European healthcare system after the infection has already been acquired elsewhere, but preventing transmission to the child depends on the possibility of being tested, diagnosed and treated in the country where the pregnancy takes place. ECDC says that effective programmes must be universal and sufficiently accessible so as not to exclude people at higher risk from screening. The standards are built around a patient-centred approach, which the agency defines through equitable access, non-discrimination, clinical relevance and services adapted to the person’s needs. This approach continues the direction established by previous European recommendations. ECDC has already supported testing for HIV, syphilis and hepatitis B during pregnancy, with repeat testing in certain risk situations and testing at delivery for people who were not tested previously. The new module shifts the focus from simply recommending screening to standardising the quality of the entire process. Each standard follows the same structure. The document provides the clinical and public health rationale, formulates a requirement concerning service quality, identifies outcomes that can be measured and establishes numerical targets where possible. The idea is that a clinic or national system should be able to verify not only whether it formally offers screening, but also whether people are tested on time and subsequently reach the services they need. This distinction is important. The existence of a national programme does not guarantee that it works for the entire population. There may be a universal screening policy while certain people do not attend prenatal care early enough, decline testing because of a lack of information, encounter administrative barriers or are not quickly connected to treatment after a positive result. For hepatitis B, ECDC reported in the summer of 2026 that all EU and EEA countries for which information was available applied universal prenatal screening for HBsAg and that most of those reporting data had reached the World Health Organization’s interim target of 90% coverage. However, the absence of data from some countries prevents a complete assessment at European level. The same analysis showed that information on treatment for eligible pregnant people with HBV infection was available for only four countries. In these countries, reported coverage was high, between 75% and 100%, but such a small sample does not allow the conclusion that the same performance exists across the EU and EEA. Standardising indicators seeks to address precisely this type of problem. If countries measure different things or report data in incompatible formats, it is difficult to determine where prevention is working well and where gaps exist. A common definition of indicators can enable more useful comparisons between systems and can turn a lack of data into a visible problem. The document also has a dimension related to eliminating vertical transmission as a public health problem. The international objective does not mean that no cases will ever occur again, but rather reducing transmission and achieving levels of coverage and performance compatible with criteria established by international organisations. For Europe, the difficulty is that a relatively low overall incidence may conceal groups or regions where access is poorer. The total number of births in the EU and EEA was approximately 3.67 million in 2023, meaning that prenatal screening programmes must operate on a very large scale even if the final number of vertical transmission cases is small relative to the population. This is also the logic behind quality indicators. A prevention programme is considered high-performing not only when the number of cases is low, but also when it can demonstrate that screening reaches the target population, results are communicated quickly, people with positive results receive the necessary intervention and children receive appropriate follow-up. The standards do not replace national clinical protocols and do not require countries to organise services in the same way. They provide a common benchmark that authorities and providers can use for evaluation and audit. The actual organisation of screening and treatment remains the responsibility of national healthcare systems. ECDC developed the module in partnership with the European AIDS Clinical Society and with clinical and public health experts from several European countries. The technical group includes specialists from Germany, Ukraine, Belgium, Bulgaria, Romania, Poland, Ireland, the Netherlands and Denmark, as well as community representation. Its publication complements a broader series of European standards for prevention and care. Previous modules addressed HIV testing, pre-exposure prophylaxis, initiation of antiretroviral therapy and management of HIV together with other conditions. The prenatal module expands the framework to a point at which prevention can simultaneously affect the health of the parent and child. The document’s significance is therefore not the introduction of a new test into European systems. Prenatal screening for these infections already exists in many countries. The innovation lies in the attempt to define at European level what a well-functioning programme means and how to measure the difference between the formal existence of screening and effective protection against vertical transmission. The seminar was jointly organised by the health ministry’s medical and public health services, the Cyprus Medical Association, the Cyprus Society of Gastroenterology, the Cyprus Society of General Medicine and the Cyprus Society of Personal and Family Doctors. Charalambides said the critical issue was shortening the path through which new medical methods and treatments reach patients. “Personal doctors have a particularly important role in this process,” he said. “Today, we have at our disposal a safe and effective vaccine for the prevention of hepatitis B, as well as treatments that can control chronic disease and reduce the risk of serious complications,” the minister said. “Modern antiviral treatments for hepatitis C achieve a cure rate of more than 95 per cent.” He warned, however, that chronic infections with the hepatitis B and C viruses can remain without obvious symptoms for long periods, meaning people who could benefit from appropriate monitoring or treatment may remain undiagnosed. As part of these efforts, the health ministry has re-established the national committee for tackling viral hepatitis and expanded the scope of its work so that it now covers all forms of viral hepatitis. The minister also addressed the social stigma surrounding viral hepatitis. “Misconceptions about the ways in which it is transmitted cause fear and discrimination and, in some cases, discourage people from getting tested or seeking medical help,” he said. “Scientifically sound information protects both public health and the dignity of patients.” Concluding, Charalambides said the goal of eliminating viral hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030 was “particularly demanding”. He said achieving it would require coordinated action by the state, healthcare professionals, scientific bodies and patient organisations. content: Skip to content Evidence Network Menu Menu Children & Youth Climate Change Healthcare Mental Health Economics Science & Tech There is new hope against hepatitis B: it’s called epigenetic editing 29 September 2026 By Dr. Kyle Muller Silencing the gene activity of the hepatitis B virus appears to prevent it from reproducing: the approach could affect latent forms of the infection. Modifying the chemical labels attached to DNA without altering its original sequence: this, in short, is the goal of epigenetic editing, an evolution of gene therapy that we can imagine as a sort of molecular switch, capable of activating or silencing the expression of a gene without modifying the genome permanently. Now this technique has been used to turn off the gene activity of the hepatitis B virus, which can remain latent in the nucleus of liver cells and which drug therapies are never able to completely inactivate. In preclinical studies, that is, not yet on human patients, epigenetic editing has been used to add chemical groups to the genome of the hepatitis B virus in infected cells, thus silencing its gene activity and preventing it from producing new viral proteins. In essence, the expression of viral genes was turned off, without however cutting the DNA double helix as is done with CRISPR/Cas9 molecular scissors, the genome editing method awarded the Nobel Prize for Chemistry in 2020 which, in some cases, can give rise to incorrect reorganizations of the chromosomes. The therapy has shown promising results in animal models, leading to profound repression of proteins (antigens) that indicate the activity of the hepatitis B virus for over six months. The results of the work, conducted by the biotechnology company nChroma Bio of Boston, the San Raffaele Telethon Institute for Gene Therapy (SR-Tiget) and the National Molecular Genetics Institute “Romeo ed Enrica Invernizzi” of Milan, were published in the scientific journal Nature Biomedical Engineering. The permanent reservoir of hepatitis B Hepatitis B is an infection that affects the liver. It is caused by the HBV virus, which is transmitted through blood or other infected body fluids (therefore also sexually) and against which a widely effective vaccine is available. In 5-10% of adult patients with hepatitis B, the disease becomes chronic, with possible very serious effects, such as liver failure (loss of liver function), cirrhosis (progressive scarring of the liver) or liver cancer. The WHO estimates that worldwide, 240 million people live with a chronic form of hepatitis B. Current pharmacological therapies are able to suppress the activity of the hepatitis B virus but not eliminate it: patients with chronic forms are therefore forced to take antivirals for life. The pathogen is in fact able to integrate into the host’s genome and deceive the immune system so as not to be attacked. One of the ways it does this is by producing free mini-chromosomes that sit in the nucleus of cells and act as genomic archives for the virus, helping it replicate again when antiviral drugs are stopped. Other pieces of the hepatitis B virus integrated into the DNA of cells also generate proteins that alter the response of immune cells to the pathogen; this form of supplementation causes molecular changes in liver cells that can cause cancer. Disable everything! The scientists used a genetic editor called CRMA-1001, capable of deactivating both persistent forms of the virus – both its permanent reservoirs and its integrations into DNA. The therapy contains an enzyme also used in the CRISPR technique, Cas9, which, however, is deprived of its “cutting” capacity; and also RNA strands that guide the enzyme to its specific targets on the viral DNA. The editor was administered as a single-dose treatment, within lipid nanoparticles, first into human liver cells, then into mice and macaques with hepatitis B. In mice, a single injection of the therapy reduced both levels of viral DNA and proteins that indicate the activity of the hepatitis B virus: in 25 of 60 rodents, both values were undetectable for more than six months. The safety of increasing doses of the medicine was investigated in macaques, with minimal and temporary adverse effects. No more drugs for life? The long-term goal is to have a gene silencer that turns off the effect of the hepatitis virus on cells with a single administration, achieving a long-lasting functional cure of the infection and freeing patients from the need to take antivirals for life. The results have given “green light” to the advancement of trials in human patients: trials are expected to begin in January in Hong Kong and New Zealand. However, it will be necessary to understand whether the therapy is able to completely eradicate the viral infection from the cells and for how long, and whether there really are no unwanted effects, even invisible ones: the equivalent of the off-target mutations of traditional CRISPR, but at the level of gene expression. And for this, it will be necessary to monitor study participants for a very long time. He earned his Ph.D. in Criminal Justice from Texas State University in 2019, where his dissertation was supervised by Dr. Scott Bowman. Dr. Mueller's research focuses on juvenile justice policies and evidence-based interventions aimed at reducing recidivism among youth offenders. His work has been instrumental in shaping data-driven strategies within the juvenile justice system, emphasizing rehabilitation and community engagement. Infectious Disease > General Infectious Disease Millions of Cancers Linked to Infections, Study Says — Four of the five leading infectious causes have "highly effective" prevention measures by Terrence Rudd, Staff Writer, MedPage Today October 1, 2026 • 3 min read Add MedPage Today on Google MedpageToday Key Takeaways Infections led to an estimated 2.3 million new cancer cases in 2024, including gastric cancer, cervical cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, leukemias and lymphomas, and nasopharyngeal cancer. Helicobacter pylori, human papillomavirus, hepatitis B virus, Epstein-Barr virus, and hepatitis C virus accounted for nearly all cancers caused by infections. Four of the five leading infectious causes of cancer, as well as HIV, already have "highly effective" prevention measures, researchers said. Over 2 million new cancer cases were attributable to infections globally in 2024, according to an analysis of worldwide cancer incidence, highlighting the importance of effective prevention measures. Infections led to an estimated 2.3 million new cancer cases in 2024, including gastric cancer, cervical cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, leukemias and lymphomas, and nasopharyngeal cancer, which accounted for 12% of all cancer cases worldwide. Among 12 carcinogenic infectious agents, the largest numbers of cancer cases were attributable to: Helicobacter pylori: 760,000 cases, population-attributable fraction (PAF) 4% Human papillomavirus (HPV): 750,000 cases, PAF 4% Hepatitis B virus (HBV): 360,000 cases, PAF 2% Epstein-Barr virus (EBV): 260,000 cases, PAF 1% Hepatitis C virus (HCV): 160,000 cases, PAF <1% Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV): 35,000 cases, PAF <1% Most cancers attributable to H. pylori were non-cardia gastric cancers (700,000 cases), while cervical cancer accounted for most HPV-attributable cases (600,000). HBV and HCV were responsible for 330,000 and 130,000 cases of hepatocellular carcinoma, respectively, while EBV led to 110,000 nasopharyngeal cancers, reported Harriet Rumgay, PhD, of the International Agency for Research on Cancer in Lyon, France, and colleagues in Lancet Oncologyopens in a new tab or window. "Our findings underscore the importance of accelerating control of infectious agents to achieve cancer prevention goals," Rumgay and colleagues wrote. Clinicians can help reach those goals through interventions such as HBV and HPV vaccination; testing and treatment for H. pylori, HBV, HCV, and HIV; and cervical screening programs, Rumgay told MedPage Today. Given those interventions, four of the five leading infectious causes of cancer, as well as HIV, already have "highly effective" prevention measures, she noted. Other measures can reduce transmission, such as safe injection practices, condom use, and HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis. The challenge lies in the infections that currently have no effective prevention tools, particularly EBV, Rumgay said. "A major priority is the development of vaccines against EBV, which causes several cancers and has also been linked to multiple sclerosis," she explained. New prevention tools are also needed for KSHV, particularly given that the KSHV-related cancer burden falls disproportionately on resource-limited countries in sub-Saharan Africa. Geography and infection prevalence present their own obstacles to taming infection-driven cancers, Rumgay added. For example, eastern Asia accounted for 42% of infection-attributable cancers in 2024, while sub-Saharan Africa was responsible for 25% of cases. In eastern Asia, H. pylori and HBV infections were behind a majority of cancer cases, while HPV was the biggest cause in sub-Saharan Africa. "As a result, prevention strategies need to be tailored to local infection and disease patterns and healthcare needs, while ensuring equitable access to effective interventions." Rumgay and colleagues analyzed 2024 national estimates of new cancer cases in people of any age from the Global Cancer Observatory's Cancer Today database and other registry data. They estimated the percentages of cases that could be attributed to 12 infectious agents classified as Group 1 carcinogens by the International Agency for Research on Cancer Monographs Program. In contrast, northern Europe (4%), and Oceania, North America, and western Europe (all 5%), were well below the 12% global PAF. Study limitations included the lack of sex-specific PAFs, which may overlook sex-related differences in the percentages of infection-attributable cancer cases. Meet the five infections responsible for almost one in eight cancers worldwide

New estimates suggest infections were responsible for 2.3 million cancer cases worldwide in 2024.

  • 30 September 2026
  • by Linda Geddes

At a glance

A new analysis by the International Agency for Research on Cancer suggests that infections caused around 12% of all new cancers worldwide in 2024, amounting to roughly 2.3 million cases.

The vast majority of these cancers were caused by Helicobacter pylori, human papillomavirus (HPV), hepatitis B, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and hepatitis C.

More than three quarters of infection-related cancers occurred in low- and middle-income countries, where many people still lack access to effective prevention and treatment.

Infections caused around 12% of all new cancers worldwide in 2024, amounting to an estimated 2.3 million cases, according to an analysis by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC).

Despite progress in vaccination and screening, infection-related cancers remain a major global challenge, with the burden falling disproportionately on populations in low- and middle-income countries.

- Dr Harriet Rumgay, IARC's Cancer Surveillance Branch

Just five infections accounted for almost all of the estimated cases: Helicobacter pylori, human papillomavirus (HPV), hepatitis B, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and hepatitis C.

Many infection-related cancers are preventable through measures such as vaccination against HPV and hepatitis B, testing and treatment for H. pylori and viral hepatitis, or screening for HPV.

However, the report warned that access to these measures remains uneven. More than three quarters (77%) of infection-related cancers occurred in low- and middle-income countries, where financial, political and health-system barriers can limit access to prevention and treatment.

Eastern Asia had the greatest number of infection-related cancers, with an estimated 990,000 cases in 2024. This accounted for 42% of the global total and was largely driven by H. pylori and hepatitis B.

However, the burden was proportionally greatest in sub-Saharan Africa, where infections were responsible for around one in four new cancer cases, particularly HPV-related cancers.

“The findings underscore the major role that infection control can play in reducing the global cancer burden,” said study co-author Dr Harriet Rumgay of the IARC's Cancer Surveillance Branch. “Despite progress in vaccination and screening, infection-related cancers remain a major global challenge, with the burden falling disproportionately on populations in low- and middle-income countries.”

So, which infections are responsible for the greatest cancer burden and what can be done about them?

Helicobacter pylori

Topping the IARC’s list was H. pylori, a bacterium found in the lining of the stomach. It is usually acquired during childhood and can persist for decades if left untreated.

Although most people who are infected never develop cancer, it can cause persistent inflammation and other changes that increase the risk of stomach cancer.

According to the IARC analysis, the bacterium was responsible for an estimated 760,000 cancer cases worldwide in 2024, around 4% of all cancers diagnosed that year.

H. pylori can be treated with antibiotics, and studies suggest that doing so can reduce the incidence of stomach cancer by 36% and deaths from the disease by 22% in people who are infected with it.

However, so far, only a few countries have implemented population-level screen-and-treat programmes for the bacterium. Vaccines against H. pylori are also in development.

Human papillomavirus (HPV)

Close behind H. pylori, HPV was responsible for an estimated 750,000 cancer cases worldwide in 2024, around 4% of all new cancers.

HPV is extremely common, with around 80% of people thought to acquire at least one infection during their lifetime. Most infections clear by themselves, but persistent infection with certain high-risk types is responsible for almost all cases of cervical cancer, as well as a proportion of anal, penile, vaginal, vulval and throat cancers.

More than two decades of research has shown that HPV vaccines substantially reduce persistent HPV infections and precancerous cervical changes. Real-world studies are also now showing that HPV vaccination is reducing cervical cancer rates in countries that introduced it early on.

Hepatitis B

Hepatitis B was responsible for an estimated 360,000 cancer cases worldwide in 2024, around 2% of all new cancers. The virus infects the liver and, if infection becomes chronic, it can cause inflammation and damage that may eventually lead to cirrhosis or liver cancer.

Hepatitis B can be prevented through vaccination. Because the risk of developing chronic hepatitis B is particularly high when infection occurs early in life, the World Health Organization recommends that all babies receive a first dose of hepatitis B vaccine within 24 hours of birth, followed by two or three further doses.

A complete course provides 98–100% protection against infection, which can last for decades and probably for life.

Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)

EBV was linked to an estimated 260,000 cancer cases in 2024, making it the fourth largest infectious cause of cancer globally. EBV is extremely common, infecting around 95% of people worldwide and remaining in the body for life.

Most infections cause few or no symptoms, although the virus can cause glandular fever if it is first encountered during adolescence or adulthood.

EBV can also contribute to the development of cancers including Burkitt lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma and nasopharyngeal cancer. The virus is also increasingly being linked to stomach cancer.

Although there is currently no licensed vaccine against EBV, several candidates are currently in development.

Hepatitis C

Hepatitis C was responsible for an estimated 160,000 cancer cases worldwide in 2024. Like hepatitis B, the virus infects the liver and can cause a persistent infection that may eventually lead to cirrhosis or liver cancer.

There is currently no vaccine against hepatitis C, although researchers are trying to develop one. However, a short course of antiviral drugs can cure more than 95% of infections and substantially reduce people's risk of developing liver cancer.

The problem is that hepatitis C can remain symptomless for many years, so many remain unaware that they are infected. Globally, access to diagnosis and treatment is also limited.

Other infectious causes of cancer

The IARC analysis included seven further infections known to cause cancer in humans. These included Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), which causes Kaposi sarcoma; human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1), which can cause a type of leukaemia; and Merkel cell polyomavirus, which is linked to a rare form of skin cancer.

The list also included three parasitic worms: Schistosoma haematobium, which is linked to bladder cancer, and the liver flukes Opisthorchis viverrini and Clonorchis sinensis, which can cause bile duct cancer. HIV was also included because, although it doesn’t directly cause cancer, the immune suppression it causes increases the risk of cancers associated with other infections.

While these infections accounted for a relatively small share of the global total, some are more important in certain regions. For example, KSHV contributed to the particularly high burden of infection-related cancers in sub-Saharan Africa, alongside HPV and HIV.

Sep 29, 2026, 9:30 PM | 3 min read Epstein-Barr Virus (Image Credit: Corona Borealis Studio/Shutterstock) Newsletter Sign up for our email newsletter for the latest science news Sign Up Epstein-Barr virus lives in nearly every adult on Earth, usually without causing any trouble. When it does lead to cancer, which cancer seems to depend on where you live. In Southeast Asia, it’s mostly tumors in the part of the throat behind the nose. In Europe and the Americas, it’s more often stomach cancer or lymphoma. That pattern shows up in a new global estimate of cancers caused by infections, published in The Lancet Oncology by researchers at the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC). The study attributes 2.3 million new cancer cases in 2024, more than a tenth of the world’s total, to infections. Epstein-Barr, the virus behind mononucleosis (mono), was linked to about 260,000 of them, a total topped only by H. pylori, HPV, and hepatitis B. “This updated analysis shows that the landscape of infection-related cancers continues to evolve as scientific evidence advances,” said Gary Clifford, senior co-author of the study, in a press release. “It also highlights where future investments in new prevention tools could have the greatest impact, particularly for infections such as EBV, for which effective vaccines are not yet available.” Why One Virus Leads to Different Cancers Once someone catches Epstein-Barr, the virus stays in their body for life, hidden inside some of their cells. Proteins the virus makes can push those cells to keep dividing, one step on the path to cancer. Explore All Options Yet only a small share of the carriers ever develop a related cancer. That gap, along with the way the cancers vary from region to region, hints that other factors are involved. Among the possibilities are people's genes, their diets and surroundings, other infections, and weakened immunity. The split is the strongest in Southeast Asia, where about 80 percent of the region’s 34,000 Epstein-Barr cancers were nasopharyngeal (the tumors that form in the upper throat behind the nose). Nasopharyngeal cancer also led in Sub-Saharan Africa. There, though, Burkitt lymphoma, a fast-growing cancer that often affects children, made up a notable share, and the authors flag malaria, widespread in the region, as a possible contributor. Stomach cancer only recently joined the list of cancers counted for Epstein-Barr in these global estimates, along with two more types of lymphoma. Those newly counted cancers make up about 100,000 of the virus’s 260,000 cases. Read More: Viagra May Limit Cancer’s Spread by Trapping Cholesterol Inside Cells The Cancers We Already Know How to Prevent Just five of the 12 infections, including Epstein-Barr, caused nearly all of the 2.3 million cases. H. pylori, a common stomach bacterium, was linked to about 760,000 cases, almost all of them stomach cancers and more than half in eastern Asia. It can be cleared with antibiotics, and stomach cancer rates have fallen in many places as sanitation has improved and fewer infections are passed between family members. HPV, linked to about 750,000 cases, is treated in the study as the cause of every cervical cancer, about 600,000 in 2024. It also causes throat, anal, and penile cancers. A single vaccine dose protects as well as two or three, which could help reach more girls in sub-Saharan Africa, where the rate of HPV-caused cancer is more than twice the global average. Hepatitis B can be prevented with a vaccine too, and antiviral drugs treat hepatitis B and C. But these tools reach some places much better than others, and low- and middle-income countries accounted for 77 percent of the cases. No Vaccines for Epstein-Barr Epstein-Barr has no vaccine or reliable way to control it once someone is infected, although several vaccines are being tested. Most people reading this probably picked up Epstein-Barr long ago, maybe from a parent’s kiss, or a shared spoon, and will never give it a second thought. A vaccine could one day let some of those who would otherwise get cancer from it do the same. This article is not offering medical advice and should be used for informational purposes only. Daily roundup Spark: Our top stories Just 5 Infections Responsible For More Than 2 Million New Cancer Cases Annually Health29 September 2026 By Jess Cockerill (Kateryna Kon/Science Photo Library RF/Getty Images) Cancer may seem like an inevitable part of life, but there are so many factors that can help reduce your risk. When we think about reducing cancer risk, we usually think of lifestyle factors: smoking, alcohol consumption, exercise. But a new study by a team of cancer epidemiologists, published in The Lancet Oncology, highlights just how much infections actually contribute to your cancer risk. Based on global data, infections were linked to 12 percent of all cancers that were diagnosed in 2024. That's 2.3 million new cancer cases. Five key pathogens were responsible for nearly all of those infection-linked cases. The most common offender was a stomach bacterium, Helicobacter pylori, which was involved in 4 percent of the total cancers diagnosed in 2024 – that's 760,000 cases. H. pylori is a really common bug: statistically speaking, every second person in the world is infected with it. For most people, infection with H. pylori causes no symptoms, but certain strains can cause gastric ulcers and ultimately stomach cancers. The human papillomavirus (HPV) was also linked to 4 percent of the total new cancers diagnosed in 2024, which is 750,000 cases. frameborder="0′′ allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen> Hepatitis B virus (HBV) was linked to 2 percent of new cases, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) was linked to 1 percent, and hepatitis C virus (HCV) was linked to less than 1 percent. EBV is a newcomer to this list. Since previous global estimates were published, the evidence that EBV causes cancer has grown substantially. It's pretty freaky to think that these infections, which can already make us very sick in their own right, could also lead to cancer, but these findings also give us an opportunity. They suggest proper treatment and prevention of these infections could make a really big difference to cancer rates across the world. "Our updated estimates highlight the continued importance of infection control in global cancer prevention strategies," lead author Harriet Rumgay and her colleagues note. "Many carcinogenic infectious agents have existing or potential preventive interventions, including vaccines, diagnostics, treatments, and safe injection practices." For many of these pathogens, it's a matter of actually getting those public health interventions to people. "Despite progress in vaccination and screening, infection-related cancers remain a major challenge globally, with persistent inequities especially impacting low-income and middle-income countries," the authors add. Three-quarters of infection-related cancers came from low-income and middle-income countries, predominantly in eastern Asia, African nations south of the Sahara, and southeastern Asia. The bulk of infection-linked cancer diagnoses in 2024 were made in eastern Asia, making up 42 percent of the global total. The infections linked to those diagnoses were mainly H. pylori and HBV. Getting more people vaccinated for HPV (especially men, who have often not been targeted for HPV vaccines) and HBV should make a huge dent in global cancer rates, but for H. pylori, the answer is not so simple. "So far, there has been little progress in developing H. pylori vaccines or highly effective H. pylori therapies that can minimize ineffective antibiotic exposure, which would be highly impactful for controlling gastric cancer globally," the authors write. We also have no vaccine or any other methods to control the spread of EBV (which infects about 95 percent of adults), though several clinical trials for vaccines are underway. "Although investment in the development of new preventive vaccinations for EBV, H. pylori, and Kaposi's sarcoma [another cancer linked to viruses] is key, many prevention strategies are known to be cost-effective," the authors write. "Unfortunately, such strategies are often underused due to societal, financial, and political barriers, often in the settings that need them most. "Considering the overwhelming economic and social costs of cancer, investment in prevention is crucial." The research was published in The Lancet Oncology. NewsPricingLoginSign up free News·Discovery Discovery nChroma Bio's epigenetic silencer therapy shows sustained HBV suppression in preclinical models Edited by Robert McTiernan·September 28, 2026·2 min read Researchers at Boston-based genetic medicines company nChroma Bio published preclinical data in Nature Biomedical Engineering supporting CRMA-1001, an LNP-delivered epigenetic silencer now in Phase I/II development for chronic hepatitis B (CHB). The study showed durable suppression of viral markers from both integrated and episomal HBV DNA without cutting the underlying DNA sequence. Why it matters: Current nucleoside/nucleotide analogue therapies suppress HBV replication but do not eliminate or durably silence the cccDNA and integrated HBV DNA reservoirs that sustain chronic infection. CRMA-1001 is designed to switch off transcription from both reservoirs through targeted DNA methylation, potentially enabling durable viral suppression from a finite treatment course. CRMA-1001 delivers mRNA encoding the EE7000 epigenetic silencer together with an HBV-targeting guide RNA in liver-directed lipid nanoparticles. The complex uses catalytically inactive Cas9 to localize transcriptional repressors and DNA methyltransferase activity to HBV DNA, depositing methylation marks without introducing DNA breaks. In mouse models, a single dose produced dose-dependent suppression of HBV antigens that persisted for up to 207 days. In an episomal HBV model, three monthly doses left approximately 90% of animals with undetectable HBsAg and HBV DNA at six months. The therapy also suppressed HBsAg and HBeAg in HBV-infected primary human hepatocytes, with methylation of cccDNA confirmed. A non-human primate toxicology program supported clinical entry, although transient liver transaminase elevations were observed at the highest tested dose. The preclinical package supported progression into a Phase I/II trial (NCT07200193), which dosed its first patient in January 2026. The study is evaluating single and multiple ascending doses in up to 66 adults with CHB who remain on background nucleoside/nucleotide analogue therapy. The AllSci BriefFree, systematic R&D and deal news. Daily. Subscribe CRMA-1001 enters an emerging field of therapies aimed directly at persistent HBV DNA reservoirs. Tune Therapeutics has already reported early clinical proof-of-concept with TUNE-401, another epigenetic silencer targeting HBV cccDNA, while Precision BioSciences is testing PBGENE-HBV, which takes a different approach by using the ARCUS nuclease platform to cut and eliminate viral DNA rather than silence it. The study was funded by nChroma Bio and included collaborators from the San Raffaele Telethon Institute for Gene Therapy and the Istituto Nazionale Genetica Molecolare in Milan. 雨露肝霖 雨露肝霖 发表于上海 慢乙肝生物标志物 消化新前沿 企业/ 关注 互相关注 2026年9月11日- 13日,“中部肝病与感染学术会议(CCIFLDI 2026)暨人畜共患传染病重症诊治全国重点实验室2026年学术会议”在湖北省武汉市隆重召开。 深度解析医学证据,DeepEvidence为你支撑决策 编者按 2026年9月11日- 13日,“中部肝病与感染学术会议(CCIFLDI 2026)暨人畜共患传染病重症诊治全国重点实验室2026年学术会议”在湖北省武汉市隆重召开。 9月12日下午,华中科技大学同济医学院附属同济医院吴迪教授进行了有关“Biomarker-Guided Therapy toward Functional Cure of Chronic Hepatitis B”的专题报告。肝霖君与您分享精彩内容。 慢乙肝难以实现临床治愈,其最大障碍不仅在于cccDNA和整合HBV DNA会持续表达HBsAg,更关键的是,在持续存在的病毒与抗原负荷下,宿主免疫系统处于一种“失能”状态。因此,亟需通过免疫调控来重塑宿主的免疫应答,从而最终抑制HBV复制,实现临床治愈。 2014年,基于OSST研究以及相应的循证医学证据,该团队提出了“免疫失能”是实现临床治愈的最大障碍,现阶段可用的核苷(酸)类似物(NA)和聚乙二醇干扰素α(PegIFNα)联合治疗可促进优势患者实现临床治愈。 基于前期开展的一系列临床试验,以及国内外的循证医学依据,由宁琴教授牵头,联合全球26位知名专家共同制定的《慢性乙型肝炎功能性治愈导航:专家共识2.0》于2025年正式发布,总结了慢乙肝临床治愈的路线图。 OSST研究:首次通过RCT研究证实,对于NAs经治、获得完全病毒学应答的慢乙肝患者,采用有限疗程的PegIFNα治疗可实现临床治愈。在停药后1年内,超过85%的患者维持HBsAg清除,实现真正的“临床治愈”。 OSST研究不仅证实了PegIFNα的治疗有效性,研究团队还据此建立了优势患者的识别方法,并提出了基线指导治疗(BGT)和应答指导治疗(RGT)策略。 Anchor研究:纳入HBsAg < 3000 IU/mL的慢乙肝患者。采用多靶点联合策略,同样以PegIFNα为核心治疗方案,延长PegIFNα疗程,并联合使用GM-CSF等免疫调节剂。 结果表明,PegIFNα + NAs组96周的HBsAg清除率超30%,HBsAb阳性率超35%。停药24周后,HBsAg清除率为27.7%,HBsAb阳性率为25.0%。 HBsAg是最关键的HBsAg清除预测指标,根据基线HBsAg水平进行分层,HBsAg < 100 IU/mL的患者HBsAg清除率为66%,100 < HBsAg < 1000 IU/mL的患者为40%。 除了HBsAg基线水平,其早期的变化幅度以及HBV RNA的早期下降幅度也可预测临床治愈率。 年龄也是一个重要的预测因素,年龄越小,越容易获得临床治愈。 结合患者治疗结束时的指标进行分析,发现治疗结束时HBcrAg < 4 log10 U/mL及HBsAb > 2 log10 mIU/mL的患者更容易维持稳定的免疫应答状态,并且更容易实现停药后持久的HBsAg清除。 系列研究证实,基于免疫调节的联合治疗策略可有效重塑宿主的免疫“失能”状态。基于此,该团队归纳总结出BGT、RGT及停药后持续应答的预测模型,并将其整合至乙肝治疗路径图中,为慢乙肝临床治疗决策提供了循证依据。 此外,HBV整合也可用于预测临床治愈。基于Anchor研究发现基线HBV整合水平越低的患者,越容易实现临床治愈。 相关免疫学指标也在持续探索中。研究发现,免疫重建不全可能是介导PegIFNα序贯治疗后病毒学复发的关键机制。此类患者的特征是单核细胞表面TLR2低水平表达,以及CD8+ T细胞表面PD-1高水平表达。 靶向上述双靶点,通过协同调节先天免疫与适应性免疫,能否进一步改善患者的治疗应答? 对此,该团队设计了一项概念验证性、小样本、探索性、RCT研究——Oceancure 05研究。纳入NA经治、HBV DNA < 20 IU/mL、250 IU/mL < HBsAg < 5000 IU/mL的慢乙肝患者,分为NAs单药治疗组、NAs + TLR7激动剂组及NAs + TLR7激动剂 + PD-L1单抗组。 结果发现,三联治疗可诱导更大幅度的HBsAg下降,平均降幅为0.45 log10 IU/mL,显著高于NAs单药组和二联治疗组。且停药后,患者的HBsAg下降幅度相对稳定,未出现大幅反弹。安全性方面,未出现严重不良反应和死亡。常见的不良反应包括甲状腺炎及ALT升高。 在该研究中发现了与PegIFNα治疗类似的现象,即早期ALT升高以及早期HBsAg的快速下降与治疗应答密切相关。 本研究检测了不同外周血单核细胞(PBMCs)表面PD-L1的表达。结果显示,NAs联合TLR7激动剂可上调各亚群PD-L1的表达,而三联治疗则能有效抑制这一上调过程。且HBsAg下降幅度越大的患者,其PD-L1下调更为显著。 研究评估了不同治疗方案下HBV特异性细胞毒性T淋巴细胞(CTL)的应答情况。结果显示,三联治疗可显著恢复HBV特异性CTL的功能。进一步分析表明,三联治疗在CTL应答的广度与强度上均显著优于二联及NAs单药治疗。此外,通过对非初始CD8+ T细胞的差异基因表达分析发现,效应相关基因呈现高表达,且PD-1阻断相关基因亦存在显著差异表达。 研究发现,在不同细胞亚群中,MDSC表面的PD-L1水平与HBV特异性CTL应答呈显著负相关,且与病毒学指标密切相关,提示该细胞亚群中的PD-1可能在三联治疗中起到核心作用。体外功能验证实验表明,在去除MDSC的培养体系中,三联治疗能显著增强PBMC的IFN分泌,并提升CTL的细胞毒性及杀伤功能。 综上,本研究证实,协同靶向天然免疫与适应性免疫可进一步促进HBsAg应答。鉴于入组患者基线HBsAg水平较高,未来需进一步优化治疗方案。 ASO(反义寡核苷酸)是靶向HBV RNA的单链核酸聚合物,可减少病毒蛋白的表达、降低HBV DNA水平,并可能通过激活TLR8通路,激活先天免疫应答。 Bepirovirsen的B-Clear研究分析发现应答人群集中在基线HBsAg低水平的患者。B-Well研究结果显示,在整个队列中,19%的患者实现临床治愈。在HBsAg < 1000 IU/mL的患者中,临床治愈率为26%。基线HBsAg水平越低,临床治愈率越高。 在其临床研究的事后分析中也发现了部分患者出现ALT 升高伴随HBsAg快速下降,提示其可能存在一定的免疫调节作用。 总结 病毒抑制联合免疫调节是目前实现临床治愈的关键策略。 整合基线、治疗早期及治疗结束后的标志物,有助于精准制定旨在实现临床治愈的联合治疗策略。 新型生物标志物,尤其是免疫学标志物,值得进一步探索,以指导新型联合治疗策略。 阅读全文 微信扫一扫 分享 版权声明:
